diagrams.title: An older app, and a failing server

elements.label: One GraphQL schema
elements.sub: shared by web, iOS and Android

shots.title: Release lag
shots.engineer: Here is a travel app's home screen: a search box, a carousel of deals, and recent trips. The layout is written into the iOS and Android code. To move deals above recent trips, the team changes both apps, builds them, and submits them to the app stores for review. Some users update within days. Many do not: Lyft has said it supports rider apps up to two years old. So for weeks, different users see different home screens.
shots.executive: On mobile, every layout change needs an app release, and users update slowly, so a change takes weeks to reach everyone.

shots.title: Flags and web views
shots.engineer: The first obvious fix is remote configuration. Build three home-screen variants into the app, and let a flag choose one. That works until someone wants a fourth variant: a new layout is new code, so it still needs a release. The second obvious fix is a web view: render an HTML page inside the app. It changes instantly, but it loads more slowly, looks out of place next to native screens, and struggles with native features.
shots.executive: Flags can only choose between layouts already shipped, and web pages inside an app feel slow and out of place.

shots.title: Describe and render
shots.engineer: Server-driven UI moves the layout decision to the server. When the traveller opens the home screen, the app asks a screen service for a description of it, and says what it can draw. The service fetches deals and trips, chooses which sections to show and in what order, checks the result against a versioned component schema, and sends it back. The app's renderer maps each section type to a native component already compiled into the app.
shots.executive: The server sends a description of the screen, and the app draws it with native building blocks it already has.

shots.title: Vocabulary
shots.engineer: The heart of it is the vocabulary: the list of component types both sides agree on, kept in a registry with a version number. Keep it closed: the server may only use types the app already knows. And keep it shallow: a screen is a list of sections, each a self-contained component with typed fields, not an arbitrary tree of boxes. Airbnb's Ghost Platform works this way, with sections, screens and actions defined in one GraphQL schema.
shots.executive: Both sides share a short, versioned list of building blocks. Keeping that list small and simple is what keeps it testable.

shots.title: Request
shots.engineer: Step by step. The app first shows the last good home screen from its own cache, so the traveller never stares at a blank page. In the background it requests the home screen, sending its schema version and the components it supports. The screen service gathers deals and recent trips and returns three sections, with their actions, as plain data. The app draws them and saves the response as the new last good screen.
shots.executive: The app shows its last copy straight away, asks the server for the latest screen, draws it, and keeps it for next time.

shots.title: Actions
shots.engineer: Behaviour is data too. Every tappable thing carries an action: navigate to a screen, open a link, save a trip, log an event. The app has a fixed set of action handlers, just as it has a fixed set of components. Tap a deal and the app runs a navigate action, which asks the server for the deal screen. Because the action is data, the server can point that button somewhere new tomorrow without a release.
shots.executive: Taps are described by the server too, so even navigation can change without an app update.

shots.title: Older app
shots.engineer: Now an older app asks for the home screen. It declares schema version five, which knows heroes and lists, but not the carousel added in version seven. The server checks the registry and degrades: it swaps the carousel for a plain list, or drops the section. If an unknown type ever slips through, the app skips it and logs it rather than crashing. And when the service is slow or down, the app keeps showing the last good screen.
shots.executive: Older apps get a simpler version of the screen, and if the server is down the app shows the last screen it had.

card.heading: Where it still goes wrong
points: A new type reaches an old client: skip it and log, never crash
A section with no sensible fallback: show an update prompt
A slow screen service delays every screen: cache and time out
A server change breaks an app version nobody tested

shots.engineer: Four things still catch teams out. A new component reaching an old client must be skipped and logged, not crash the app. Some sections have no sensible fallback, so the server needs to know which app versions support what, and may show an update prompt instead. Every screen now waits on a server call, so the timeout and the cache matter. And a server change can break an app version nobody tested.
shots.executive: The danger moves from slow releases to untested combinations of server and app versions.

card.heading: What you gain, what you pay
points: Gain | Cost
Layout changes ship in minutes | Each change can break every live app version
One screen logic for iOS, Android and web | A renderer and registry to build and own
Experiments without a release | The screen is now data, so harder to test
Native look and speed | Rich interaction and animation stay hard

shots.engineer: The trade-offs. Layout changes ship in minutes, but every change can now break every app version in the field. One screen logic can serve iOS, Android and web, but you build and own a renderer and a registry on each. Experiments no longer need a release, but the screen is data now, which is harder to test. And you keep a native look and speed, while rich interaction and animation stay hard.
shots.executive: You trade slow releases for a platform you must build, own and test carefully.

card.heading: Testing across clients
points: Contract tests: every response validates against the schema
Snapshot every component on each supported app version
Preview screens before they go live
Roll out screen changes gradually and watch crash rates

shots.engineer: Testing changes shape. Contract tests check that every server response matches the schema, and that the schema never removes something an old app still needs. Snapshot tests render each component on every supported app version. A preview tool lets people see a screen before it goes live. And screen changes roll out gradually, like any release, with crash rates and errors watched by app version.
shots.executive: Every server response is checked against the shared schema, and changes go out gradually.

card.heading: When not to use it
points: Highly interactive screens: maps, editors, games
Small teams with one platform and frequent releases
Screens that rarely change
As a general UI language with arbitrary nesting

shots.engineer: When not to use it. Highly interactive screens, such as maps, editors or games, need real client code. A small team on one platform that releases often gains little and pays for a whole framework. Stable screens that rarely change do not need it. And do not grow it into a general UI language: Thoughtworks' Technology Radar warns of overly configurable messes, and of a god protocol that becomes hard to maintain.
shots.executive: Use it for screens that change often, not for highly interactive ones, and not as a general-purpose UI language.

shots.title: Who uses it
shots.engineer: In the wild. Airbnb described its Ghost Platform in 2021: sections, screens and actions, defined in one shared GraphQL schema and rendered on web, iOS and Android. Lyft's bikes and scooters team wrote about moving to server-driven UI, using semantic components and actions defined in protobuf. Microsoft's Adaptive Cards are a public example: JSON cards that Teams and Outlook render natively, with a version, a fallback and a requires property for clients that lack a feature.
shots.executive: Airbnb, Lyft and Microsoft's Adaptive Cards all use the idea, and Thoughtworks recommends it for dynamic areas only.

shots.title: Neighbours
shots.engineer: Its neighbours. The screen service is often a backend for frontend, shaped for one client. Feature flags decide which screen description a user receives, which makes experiments cheap. Contract testing keeps the schema honest so old apps keep working. Graceful degradation is how older clients get a simpler screen rather than an error. And web views are the alternative: instant changes, but without the native feel.
shots.executive: It works with backends for frontends, feature flags, contract tests and graceful degradation.

card.heading: Recap
points: The server describes the screen; the app draws it natively
Keep the vocabulary closed, versioned and shallow
Degrade for old clients, and test every live version

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. The server describes the screen and the app draws it from native components it already has, so layouts change without a release. Keep the vocabulary closed, versioned and shallow, so it stays testable. And plan for old clients: they declare what they support, the server degrades for them, and contract tests protect every app version still in use.
shots.executive: The server describes, the app draws. Keep the building blocks few. Look after older app versions.

meta.blurb: Ship screen layouts from the server, rendered with native components the app already has.
